docs.title: Redis Agent Memory for n8n
docs.text:
Memory for n8n AI Agents, backed by Redis Agent Memory: session history with server-side summaries, long-term memory the agent can search and save, and the operations to manage both from a workflow.

Installing @redis/n8n-nodes-agent-memory adds three entries to n8n's node picker. Two of them are the same node shown in two places.

Shown in n8n as Kind Where you find it Who runs it Redis Agent Chat Memory memory sub-node the AI Agent's Memory input (AI → Memory → Other memories) the AI Agent, on every turn: it loads the history before the model runs and saves the turn after Redis Agent Memory action node the main node list, wired into the workflow like any other node the workflow, one operation per execution Redis Agent Memory Tool tool sub-node the AI Agent's Tool input the model, when it decides a call is needed

Redis Agent Memory and Redis Agent Memory Tool are one node: n8n lists an action node that is usable as a tool under both names. Chat Memory Manager, mentioned in the guide, is n8n's own node and not part of this package.

  • Redis Agent Chat Memory holds the conversation. Recent turns go back to the model; the server folds older turns into a summary and extracts lasting facts about the user into long-term memory, which the node can recall on every turn.
  • Redis Agent Memory manages long-term memories, sessions, namespaces and summary views, one operation per REST call. As Redis Agent Memory Tool the same operations are available to the agent, so it can search and save memories when it decides to.

The package calls the Agent Memory REST API through n8n's own HTTP helpers, has no runtime dependencies, and passes n8n's strict (Cloud-eligible) lint rules.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
• Installation - supported versions, how to install the community node, and how to create the credential.
  • Quick Start - give an AI Agent memory in five steps and see a fact survive a new conversation.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
• Users, Sessions and Namespaces - the three identifiers that decide who sees what: the User ID that isolates users, the session that holds a conversation, and the namespace that groups memories for sharing.
  • Chat Memory - the memory sub-node: what the model is given, how the context window is trimmed, what n8n's Chat Memory Manager node can and cannot do.
  • Action Node and Tools - the resources and operations, how to pin a tool for an agent, and what the simplified output looks like.
  • Summary Views - standing summaries the server keeps per user, session, namespace or memory type, for hand-off notes, digests and standing briefings.
  • Memory Sources - where a memory came from: the session and the events it was extracted from, for citations, audit and clean-up.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Example workflows - six workflows to import, each built for a gap n8n users ask about: an agent with long-term memory, session lifecycle, shared memory across agents, hand-off packets and digests, tracing and correcting memories, and importing history.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Operations - every resource, operation and field of the action node and the chat memory node.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: • Development - building, linting, the three test layers, and where the design notes live.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: The repository is a standard n8n community node package built with @n8n/node-cli. Guidance for contributors is in CONTRIBUTING.md; this page is the short version.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
npm install
npm run dev        # builds and starts n8n with this node at http://localhost:5678
npm run lint       # n8n community-node lint rules (must pass for verification)
npm run format     # prettier over the TypeScript and JavaScript sources; CI checks this
npm run build
npm run ci         # everything CI runs: ci:build, then ci:e2e
npm run ci:build   # the CI workflow: format:check, lint, typecheck, test:coverage, build
npm test           # unit tests, no network
npm run test:coverage  # the same, with a coverage report in coverage/
npm run e2e:up     # n8n in Docker with this package, for manual testing at http://127.0.0.1:15678
npm run e2e:down   # stop it
npm run ci:e2e     # the E2E workflow: test:contract, then test:e2e

npm run dev runs n8n in a container from n8n 3.0 onward, so Docker or Podman is required. Use npx n8n-node dev --external-n8n to attach to your own instance.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• No runtime dependencies. The node calls the Agent Memory REST API through n8n's HTTP helpers, not through the @redis-iris/agent-memory SDK. @n8n/ai-node-sdk and n8n-workflow are peer dependencies provided by n8n.
  • Strict lint rules. The package passes n8n's Cloud-eligible rules; every lint and type warning is addressed rather than disabled.
  • The node never reads the environment. Only the test harness does; n8n verification forbids it in nodes.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Three layers, from fast to realistic. The full description, including the Docker stack and the LLM stub, is in docs/testing.md.

Layer Command Needs What it checks Unit npm test Nothing The chat history and memory classes, supplyData, the action node's execute, and the credential's test request, against fake HTTP Contract npm run test:contract Agent Memory The same against the real REST API, without n8n End-to-end npm run test:e2e Agent Memory, Docker The built package inside a real n8n, driven through webhooks Manual npm run e2e:up / npm run e2e:down Docker The same n8n, kept running for you to use in a browser

Contract and end-to-end tests read AGENT_MEMORY_SERVER_URL, AGENT_MEMORY_STORE_ID and AGENT_MEMORY_API_KEY from the environment or a .env file (copy .env.example). Without them they skip. Tests that wait for the server's asynchronous work (summaries, summary views, extraction) are opt-in behind AGENT_MEMORY_SUMMARY_TESTS, AGENT_MEMORY_SUMMARY_VIEW_TESTS and AGENT_MEMORY_EXTRACTION_TESTS.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from docs/ and mkdocs.yml. To preview it:

uvx --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve

or, with pip, pip install -r docs/requirements.txt && mkdocs serve. The Documentation workflow builds the site in strict mode on every pull request that touches it and deploys main to GitHub Pages with mike as the latest version.

The working documents behind the node live next to the site but are not part of it: docs/design-draft.md holds the background and design decisions, and docs/0.3.0-features.md the feature specifications. examples/ holds the workflows the Examples page describes; when a node parameter changes, import them into n8n again to check that they still load and run.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: Releases are published to npm only from GitHub Actions, with npm provenance and Trusted Publishing; the repository holds no npm token. There is no changelog file: GitHub generates the release notes from the pull request titles since the last release. The steps are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Example Workflows
docs.text: Six workflows in examples/, ready to import. Each was built for a gap that n8n users ask about most, as measured in a survey of the n8n forum, GitHub issues and 1,197 memory templates in November 2026: 86% of memory templates use a sliding window only, long-term memory is hand-built from Google Sheets and Postgres with a "Save Memory" tool the model often never calls, and the most-viewed threads ask for session resets, memory that several agents share without leaking between customers, a way to trace and correct what was learned, hand-off notes and digests, and a way to import history.

docs.title: Importing a workflow
docs.text:
1. In n8n, open Workflows → Create and choose Import from URL… or Import from File… from the workflow menu (the ⋯ at the top right of the editor).
  2. Use the file's raw URL, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redis/n8n-nodes-agent-memory/main/examples/<name>.json, or download the file and pick it.
  3. Open every Redis node and select your Redis Agent Memory API credential; where an agent is involved, select an OpenAI credential on the chat model node.
  4. Read the sticky note in the workflow. It holds the steps to try.

The examples use a demo User ID (demo-user in a Set node, a webhook body, or sample rows). In your workflow, take it from the authenticated trigger: a Telegram or Slack sender ID, a JWT claim, the n8n user. Never from the message body.

Workflow Gap it closes Node features Agent with long-term memory Facts that outlive the conversation, without a hand-built memory store Chat memory with recall, Search and Create as tools Session lifecycle /reset, "forget me", expire idle sessions Session → Get Many and Delete, Long-Term Memory → Get Many and Delete Shared memory across agents Two agents on one customer, no bleed between customers Namespace → Create, the chat memory's Namespace ID option, namespace-scoped tools Hand-off packet and weekly digest Human-readable summaries on demand Summary View → Create, Refresh and Get Result Trace, correct and forget Audit, corrections, poisoning triage Search with Include Sources, Session → Get, Update, Session → Get Many, delete by Session ID Backfill history Import a year of conversations and known facts Session → Add Event with Created At, Long-Term Memory → Create with topics

docs.title: Agent with long-term memory
docs.text: File: agent-with-long-term-memory.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: The top long-term-memory template on n8n.io and the most-watched tutorials all build the same thing by hand: extract facts about the user from each conversation and recall them on the next one, with a spreadsheet or a database as the store and 20 to 100 extra nodes. This workflow is that pattern with the store, the extraction and the recall on the server.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T[Chat Trigger] --> I[Identify the user]
    I --> A[AI Agent]
    M[OpenAI Chat Model] -.-> A
    R[Redis Agent Chat Memory<br/>recall on] -.-> A
    S[Search memories<br/>tool] -.-> A
    V[Save memory<br/>tool] -.-> A
  • Identify the user (Set) pins userId to demo-user and passes the chat fields through.
  • Redis Agent Chat Memory stores each turn in the session and, with Recall Long-Term Memories on, searches the user's memories with the current message on every turn and gives the hits to the model.
  • Search memories is a Redis Agent Memory Tool set to Long-Term Memory → Search with the User ID pinned to the Set node's value and the Query left to the model. The agent uses it when a question depends on history.
  • Save memory is the same node set to Long-Term Memory → Create, Text left to the model. The agent uses it to remember a fact at once, without waiting for extraction.
  • The system message tells the model when to use each tool.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Say: I'm vegetarian and I live in Sofia.
  2. Start a new chat, which is a new session, and ask: What should I cook tonight?

The answer uses what you said before: the agent saved it with Save memory, the server also extracted it on its own, and the memory node recalled it for the new turn.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Replace the Set node's constant with an expression over the trigger. Keep User ID pinned on both tools. If you only want recall and no tools, delete the two tool nodes; if you want the agent in full control, turn recall off and keep them.

docs.title: Session lifecycle
docs.text: File: session-lifecycle.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: "How do I clear a session key?", "reset memory", "delete all memories": the three most-viewed memory threads on the n8n forum (6,900, 5,735 and 4,774 views) are about the lifecycle of a conversation, and the built-in memory nodes offer nothing beyond letting the session expire. This workflow gives a chat bot /reset and /forget me, and a nightly job that expires idle sessions.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T[Chat Trigger] --> I[Identify the user] --> W{Route commands}
    W -->|/reset| D1[Session → Delete] --> R1[Reply: session cleared]
    W -->|/forget me| L1[Session → Get Many<br/>by User ID] --> X1{Any?} -->|yes| D2[Session → Delete]
    X1 -->|no| L2
    D2 --> L2[Long-Term Memory → Get Many<br/>by User ID] --> X2{Any?} -->|yes| D3[Long-Term Memory → Delete] --> R2[Reply: forgotten]
    X2 -->|no| R2
    W -->|anything else| A[AI Agent]
    N[Every night 03:00] --> L3[Session → Get Many<br/>all] --> F[Idle for 30 days] --> D4[Session → Delete]
  • Route commands (Switch) compares the trimmed, lower-cased message with /reset and /forget me; everything else goes to the agent.
  • /reset: Delete this session removes the current session with its events and summary. Long-term facts stay, and the reply says so.
  • /forget me: List my sessions (Session → Get Many, User ID filter, Return All) and Delete session for each; then List my memories (Long-Term Memory → Get Many, User ID filter, Return All, Execute Once) and Delete memory for each. The two Any …? IF nodes handle a user with nothing to delete: the Get Many nodes have Always Output Data on, so an empty list still produces one (empty) item and the flow reaches the reply.
  • The agent branch is the Quick Start wiring with recall on.
  • Every night at 03:00 (Schedule Trigger) → List all sessions (Session → Get Many without filters, Return All) → Idle for 30 days (Filter on updatedAt, falling back to createdAt) → Delete idle session.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Chat: I'm Ana and I prefer short answers.
  2. Send /reset, then ask What do you know about me? The fact survives the reset.
  3. Send /forget me, then ask again. Nothing is left.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Change the 30 days in the Filter node, or filter by ownerId to expire one tenant's sessions. For a Telegram or Slack bot, the Switch works on the message text the same way. If sessions are shared (group chats), turn /forget me into an admin-only command: it deletes by User ID, and in a shared session that is every participant's memories.

docs.title: Shared memory across agents
docs.text: File: shared-memory-across-agents.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: Multi-channel and multi-agent builds (a sales bot and a support bot on the same customer, a clinic on WhatsApp and Telegram) are among the most-discussed memory problems in the forum: either each agent forgets what the other learned, or one customer's facts leak into another's chat, and the templates that solve it run to 58–84 nodes. Here both agents write to and recall from one shared namespace while the User ID keeps customers apart inside it. Each agent keeps its own session, so conversation history does not mix.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Set up once] --> C[Namespace → Create<br/>customer-facts, Shared]
    T[Chat Trigger] --> N[Namespace → Get Many] --> P[Pick customer-facts] --> I[Identify the customer] --> W{Which team?}
    W -->|sales:| A1[Sales agent]
    W -->|otherwise| A2[Support agent]
    M1[Sales memory<br/>namespace set] -.-> A1
    M2[Support memory<br/>namespace set] -.-> A2
    L[OpenAI Chat Model] -.-> A1 & A2
    T1[Search shared memories] -.-> A1 & A2
    T2[Save shared memory] -.-> A1 & A2
  • Set up once (Manual Trigger) → Create the shared namespace: Namespace → Create, name customer-facts, scope Shared. Run it once.
  • On each chat message, Find namespaces and Pick customer-facts look the namespace up by name, and Identify the customer (Set) carries userId, namespaceId, sessionId and chatInput forward. The lookup is there so the example runs without pasting IDs; see below.
  • Which team? (Switch) sends messages that start with sales: to the Sales agent and everything else to the Support agent. Each agent strips the prefix from the prompt.
  • Sales memory and Support memory are two chat memory nodes with different Session ID prefixes (sales-…, support-…) and the same Namespace ID option, so extracted facts from both land in customer-facts and recall searches it.
  • Search shared memories and Save shared memory are tools attached to both agents, with the User ID pinned and the namespace set under Options (Search) and Additional Fields (Create).

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Run Set up once.
  2. Chat: sales: We are a team of 12 and our budget is 500 a month.
  3. New chat: support: Which plan fits us? The support agent knows the team size and budget it was never told.
  4. Change userId in Identify the customer to other-customer and ask again: nothing is known.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: In production, store the namespace ID once (a Set node, a workflow variable) and delete the two lookup nodes; one list request per turn is wasteful. Give each channel its own trigger and keep the Switch, or drop the Switch and run one agent per workflow with the same namespace. A Personal namespace per customer is the alternative when teams must not share a pool at all; Long-Term Memory → Move promotes a memory from one namespace to another.

docs.title: Hand-off packet and weekly digest
docs.text: File: handoff-packet-and-weekly-digest.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: The best bot-to-human hand-off template on n8n.io (17,900 views, 39 nodes) has the human type the summary of what the bot learned, and "what did the agent learn this week" digests are built from dozens of nodes. A summary view is a standing summary the server keeps per user, so both become a few nodes.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Set up once] --> C[Summary View → Create<br/>customer-briefing, by User, Manual]
    W[POST /webhook/handoff] --> F1[Find views] --> P1[Pick customer-briefing] --> R1[Refresh<br/>Partition, Wait For Result] --> H[Hand-off packet] --> O[Respond]
    K[Every Monday 08:00] --> F2[Find views] --> P2[Pick customer-briefing] --> R2[Refresh<br/>Full] --> L[Session → Get Many] --> U[Known users only] --> D[One item per user] --> G[Get Result<br/>Wait For Result] --> E[Digest line] --> A[Collect all lines] --> Z[Weekly digest]
  • Set up once → Create the briefing view: Summary View → Create, name customer-briefing, Group By User, Output Format Text, Refresh Mode Manual, with instructions for a briefing under 150 words for a human agent taking over.
  • Hand-off packet. POST /webhook/handoff with { "userId": "demo-user" }. Find views and Pick customer-briefing look the view up by name; Refresh this customer's briefing runs a Partition refresh for the Group ownerId from the request with Wait For Result on (up to 90 seconds); Hand-off packet (Set) shapes userId, briefing, status, memoriesSummarized, computedAt; Respond with the packet returns it, ready for a Zendesk or HubSpot note.
  • Weekly digest. Every Monday at 08:00 → look the view up → Refresh every briefing (Full) → List sessions (Session → Get Many, Return All) → Known users only (Filter: has ownerId) → One item per user (Remove Duplicates on ownerId) → Read the user's briefing (Get Result with Wait For Result, up to 120 seconds, for each user) → Digest line (Set: user and text, or "(nothing learned yet)" for an EMPTY result) → Collect all lines (Aggregate) → Weekly digest (Set: one Markdown document). Connect Slack or Gmail after it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Run Set up once.
  2. Chat with any agent example in this folder as demo-user.

  3. Open Respond with the packet and choose Execute step. Escalation request carries a pinned sample request, so the hand-off branch runs in the editor without a client:

    {
  "userId": "demo-user",
  "ticketId": "HD-48213",
  "channel": "chat",
  "reason": "Customer asked for a human agent"
}

    Only userId is read; the other fields show what a help-desk escalation carries. Pinned data applies to editor runs only. To call the live webhook instead, activate the workflow and send the same body:

    curl -X POST https://your-n8n/webhook/handoff \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"userId": "demo-user"}'

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Summary views must be enabled on the store. In production the View field offers the store's views in a list, so pick the view there and drop the lookup nodes. Switch the view to Continuous refresh if the briefing must be fresh without a Refresh step; it costs a model call per change. For a structured hand-off (fields for a CRM), create a second view with Output Format Structured and a schema. To give the agent itself the briefing on every turn, set the chat memory node's Summary View ID option to the view's ID.

docs.title: Trace, correct and forget
docs.text: File: trace-and-correct-a-memory.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: Corrections ("I moved from Berlin to Madrid"), audit ("which conversation produced this?") and memory poisoning (a feature request on the n8n forum, and the core failure mode named by two 2026 benchmarks) all need to know where a memory came from. No other n8n memory node shows it; Mem0 carries three open requests for exactly this. Every memory here carries its sources: the session and the exact events it was extracted from.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Three HTTP endpoints an operator or an admin workflow can call.

flowchart LR
    W1[POST /webhook/memory/trace] --> S[Search<br/>Include Sources] --> H{Session source?} -->|yes| R[Session → Get<br/>Include Summarized Events] --> E[Evidence report] --> M[Merge] --> O1[Respond]
    H -->|no| N[No sources] --> M
    W2[POST /webhook/memory/correct] --> S2[Search<br/>limit 1] --> F2{Found?} -->|yes| U[Long-Term Memory → Update] --> O2[Respond]
    F2 -->|no| O5[Respond: nothing matched]
    W3[POST /webhook/memory/forget-thread] --> L1[Session → Get Many<br/>by User ID] --> P[Pick the thread] --> D1[Session → Delete] --> L[Long-Term Memory → Get Many<br/>by Session ID and User ID] --> X{Anything?} -->|yes| D2[Long-Term Memory → Delete] --> O3[Respond: count]
    X -->|no| O4[Respond: 0]
  • Trace. { "userId": "demo-user", "query": "where does the user live" }. Search with sources finds up to three memories with Include Sources on, which puts each memory's sources (kind, session, eventIds) on the record with no extra request. Has a session source? (IF) splits them: with one, Read the session gets the session with Include Summarized Events on, so evidence is found even after the session was summarized, and Evidence report (Set) pairs the memory with the events whose IDs are in eventIds, as role (time): text lines; without one, No sources (Set) reports the memory with a note, since a memory created directly, by a Save tool for instance, has nothing that extracted it. Collect the report (Merge) joins both, and the response lists every memory. Always Output Data on the search makes an empty match answer too.
  • Correct. { "userId": "demo-user", "query": "where does the user live", "text": "The user lives in Madrid." }. Find the memory is Search with Limit 1 for the user, by query or, when there is none, by the new text itself, which finds the closest existing fact; Found one? (IF) guards it; Rewrite the memory is Long-Term Memory → Update with the new Text; the memory keeps its ID and sources. No match answers { "corrected": false }.
  • Forget a thread. { "userId": "demo-user", "sessionId": "…" }. The user's sessions (Session → Get Many by User ID), Collect sessions (Aggregate) and Pick the thread (Set) choose the session: the one named in the request, or the user's most recently updated one when none is. Then Delete the session, Memories extracted from it (Get Many with the Session ID and User ID filters, Return All, Always Output Data), Anything to delete? (IF) and Delete memory for each; the response reports memoriesDeleted.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Seed memories first by chatting with another example as demo-user; extraction takes up to a minute or two. Each webhook carries a pinned sample request for demo-user, so the three flows run in the editor without a client:

  1. Open Respond with the report and choose Execute step. The pinned request is { "userId": "demo-user", "query": "where does the user live" }; the report lists each matching memory with its evidence, or with a note when nothing extracted it.
  2. Open Respond with the memory and choose Execute step. The pinned request is { "userId": "demo-user", "query": "where does the user live", "text": "The user lives in Madrid." }. Run the trace again to see the corrected text.
  3. Open Respond: thread forgotten and choose Execute step. The pinned request is { "userId": "demo-user" }, so the user's most recent session and the memories extracted from it go; add a sessionId from the report to pick a thread. Run the trace once more to see that they are gone.

Pinned data applies to editor runs only. To call the live endpoints, activate the workflow and send the same bodies:

curl -X POST https://your-n8n/webhook/memory/trace \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"userId": "demo-user", "query": "where does the user live"}'

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Put the webhooks behind header or JWT authentication: they read and delete user data. For a review queue of facts from an untrusted channel, run the trace on Get Many with the Session ID filter instead of Search. Document sources (kind: DOCUMENT) appear once a store ingests documents; the Filter node leaves them out of the session trace.

docs.title: Backfill history
docs.text: File: backfill-history.json

docs.title: The gap
docs.text: "How do I import a year of chat history?" is a recurring forum question (3,303 and 2,268 views on the top threads), and a new deployment that knows nothing about returning customers is a poor first impression. Two import paths, one node each.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R[Run once] --> C1[Past conversations<br/>sample rows] --> E[Session → Add Event<br/>with Created At] --> W[Wait 90 s] --> S[Search<br/>Include Sources]
    R --> C2[Known facts<br/>sample rows] --> M[Long-Term Memory → Create<br/>with Topics]
  • Past conversations (sample rows) (Code) yields six rows of two old conversations: sessionId, userId, role, text, createdAt.
  • Replay into sessions is Session → Add Event per row, with Created At under Additional Fields set from the row, so the events keep their original timestamps. The server summarizes the sessions and extracts long-term facts from them, exactly as for a live chat.
  • Known facts (sample rows) (Code) yields three CRM-style facts with topics.
  • Write facts as memories is Long-Term Memory → Create per row, with Topics under Additional Fields. No extraction wait: the facts are searchable at once.
  • Wait for extraction gives the server 90 seconds, then What is remembered now? searches the user's memories with Include Sources on: the imported facts (no sources) and the extracted ones (each pointing at the imported session it came from).

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Run the workflow. Then chat with any agent example as demo-user: it knows Maria's bakery, the vegan menu and the Monday closing.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text: Replace the two Code nodes with Google Sheets, Postgres, a CSV through Extract From File, or your CRM, and keep the column names. Add Namespace ID under Additional Fields on both Redis nodes to import into a namespace. Role values are USER, ASSISTANT and SYSTEM. Each row is one request; for very large imports, run the workflow in batches with Loop Over Items.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Dependency Supported versions n8n 2.42.6 tested by the end-to-end suite, and nightly on the latest release; releases that ship @n8n/ai-node-sdk @n8n/ai-node-sdk 0.32.4 or later, provided by n8n Redis Agent Memory a store on an Agent Memory service, with an API key

Older n8n versions that ship @n8n/ai-node-sdk may work but are not tested.

docs.title: Install the node
docs.text:
n8n UICommand lineFrom source
  1. Open Settings → Community Nodes.
  2. Choose Install, enter @redis/n8n-nodes-agent-memory, accept the risk notice and install.
  3. Three entries appear in the node picker: Redis Agent Chat Memory under AI → Memory, Redis Agent Memory in the main node list, and Redis Agent Memory Tool in the AI Agent's Tool picker.

This is the path for self-hosted n8n and for n8n Cloud once the node is verified. See the n8n community nodes guide for the current rules.

In the n8n installation directory (for Docker, inside the container's ~/.n8n/nodes folder):

npm install @redis/n8n-nodes-agent-memory

Restart n8n afterwards.

git clone https://github.com/redis/n8n-nodes-agent-memory.git
cd n8n-nodes-agent-memory
npm install
npm run dev        # builds and starts n8n with this node at http://localhost:5678

npm run dev runs n8n in a container from n8n 3.0 onward, so Docker or Podman is required. Use npx n8n-node dev --external-n8n to attach to an n8n you already run.

Upgrading from 0.3.0 or earlier

Version 0.4.0 renames two identifiers that n8n stores in workflow JSON, before the node is verified for n8n Cloud and the names are fixed for good:

  • The chat memory sub-node's type is now redisAgentChatMemory (was redisAgentMemoryChatMemory). A workflow saved with an earlier version shows that node as unknown; delete it, add Redis Agent Chat Memory again and set its parameters.
  • The User ID parameter of Redis Agent Chat Memory and of Session → Add Event is stored as ownerId (was actorId), the key every other operation already uses. A saved value under the old key is ignored, so open those nodes and set User ID again.

The display names, the credential and the stored data are unchanged.

docs.title: Create the credential
docs.text:
Both nodes use one credential, Redis Agent Memory API, with three fields:

Field Where to find it Server URL AI Services / Iris / Agent Memory page, Configuration tab, General Settings. Enter the host only (https://…), without a path: the nodes add /iris/data/v1/agent-memory themselves. Store ID Same page and tab. API Key AI Services / Iris / Agent Memory page, API Keys tab.

The credential test calls the store's health endpoint, so a wrong URL, store or key fails at save time rather than at the first chat.

Summary views and extraction

Long-term memory extraction and summary views are features of the store. Extraction is on by default on hosted stores; summary views must be enabled on the store before the Summary View resource and the chat memory's Summary View ID option work.

Next: the Quick Start.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Give an AI Agent memory that outlives the conversation, in five steps.

docs.title: 1. Build the workflow
docs.text:
1. Add a Chat Trigger and an AI Agent node, and connect a chat model (for example OpenAI).
  2. Attach Redis Agent Chat Memory to the Agent's Memory input and select your Redis Agent Memory credential.
  3. Set User ID to a stable identifier for the end user. Take it from the authenticated trigger (a JWT claim, a Telegram or Slack sender ID), not from the message body: the User ID is what keeps one user's memories away from another.
  4. Leave Session ID at its default, {{ $json.sessionId }}, which the Chat Trigger provides.
  5. Turn on Recall Long-Term Memories.
flowchart LR
    T[Chat Trigger] --> A[AI Agent]
    M[OpenAI Chat Model] -.->|model| A
    R[Redis Agent Chat Memory] -.->|memory| A

docs.title: 2. Chat
docs.text:
Say something worth remembering:

I'm vegetarian and I live in Sofia.

Recent turns are replayed to the model on each message. Older turns are folded into a server-side summary, and the server extracts lasting facts from the conversation into long-term memory, asynchronously.

docs.title: 3. Start a new conversation
docs.text:
Open a new chat, which is a new session, and ask:

What should I cook tonight?

With Recall Long-Term Memories on, the memory node searches the user's long-term memories with the current message and gives the hits to the model before the conversation. The answer uses what you said in the first session.

Extraction takes a moment

Facts said in this turn may not be searchable until the next one; on the hosted store extraction has taken from 17 seconds to a minute or more. If the second chat does not know yet, wait and ask again.

docs.title: 4. Let the agent decide
docs.text:
Recall on every turn is the simplest wiring. For an agent that looks things up on purpose and saves facts right away, attach Redis Agent Memory Tool nodes to the Agent's Tool input:

  • Search memories: Long-Term Memory → Search, User ID fixed to the same expression as the memory node, Query left to the model.
  • Save memory: Long-Term Memory → Create, User ID fixed, Text left to the model.

Both can be combined with recall. Never let the model fill User ID.

docs.title: 5. Import the finished example
docs.text: examples/agent-with-long-term-memory.json is this workflow, ready to import: select your credentials and chat. The Examples page walks through it and five more.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Users, Sessions and Namespaces explains the identifiers you just set.
  • Chat Memory covers the context window, the summary and the other options.
  • Action Node and Tools lists what a workflow can do with memories, sessions and namespaces.

docs.title: Action Node and Tools
docs.text: One node with two faces. In the node list it is Redis Agent Memory, an action node the workflow runs to manage what the memory sub-node writes. In an AI Agent's Tool picker n8n lists the same node as Redis Agent Memory Tool, a tool sub-node the model calls when it decides to search or save a memory. Each operation is one REST call on the credential's store.

docs.title: Resources and operations
docs.text:
Resource Operations Long-Term Memory Search (by meaning, for one user), Get Many (by filters), Create, Get, Get Sources (the sessions or documents a memory came from), Update, Delete, Move (to another namespace) Session Get, Get Many, Delete, Add Event, Delete Event Namespace Create, Get, Get Many, Update, Delete Summary View Get Result (one group's summary), Refresh, Create, Get, Get Many, Update, Delete

Every field of every operation is listed in the Operations reference.

docs.title: Using the node as a tool
docs.text:
Attach one Redis Agent Memory Tool per operation to the Agent's Tool input and pin everything but the content: set Resource, Operation and User ID yourself, and let the model fill Query (Search) or Text (Create) with Let the model define this parameter. Two instances cover most agents:

  • Search memories: Long-Term Memory → Search, User ID fixed. The agent calls it when it needs something it was told before.
  • Save memory: Long-Term Memory → Create, User ID fixed. The agent calls it to remember a fact right away, without waiting for extraction.

Never let the model fill User ID

The User ID is what keeps one user's memories away from another. Set it from the workflow, for example {{ $('Identify the user').item.json.userId }}.

Extraction is asynchronous, so a fact said in this turn may not be searchable until the next one; Save memory is how an agent makes a fact available at once.

Other safe tools: Get Sources and Search with Include Sources (read-only, lets the agent cite where it learned something) and Summary View → Get Result with the view and the User ID group pinned ("what do you know about me?" in one call).

docs.title: Search and Get Many
docs.text:
Search ranks a user's memories by meaning against a Query and returns up to Limit results (1–100). Options narrow it: Memory Type, Namespace ID, Session ID, Topics (any of a comma-separated list) and a Similarity Threshold between 0 and 1 (0 returns the closest matches regardless of score).

Get Many lists memories by filters alone, without a query: User ID, Memory Type, Namespace ID, Session ID, Topics. At least one filter is required. It pages through the server's results with Return All or Limit. Use it for clean-up ("every memory from this session") and audits; use Search when a question is involved.

docs.title: Create, Update, Delete and Move
docs.text:
• Create stores a Text for a User ID, with optional Memory ID, Memory Type, Namespace ID, Session ID and Topics. Creating the same Memory ID again replaces the memory, which is how a workflow keeps a single fact current.
  • Update changes any of the same fields on an existing memory. Topics replaces the existing topics.
  • Delete removes one memory. Deletion is permanent.
  • Move places a memory in another namespace, chosen from the store's list or given as an ID or expression.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Every operation that returns records has a Simplify switch, on by default, which keeps the fields a workflow usually needs:

Record Simplified fields Memory memoryId, text, ownerId, memoryType, topics, namespaceId, sessionId, createdAt; with Include Sources on (Search, Get, Get Many), sources: sourceId, kind, sessionId or documentId, eventIds Source (Get Sources) sourceId, kind, sessionId, documentId, revision, eventIds (every event behind the source, in one list), evidenceCount (the number of evidence entries, not of events), capturedAt (when the first evidence entry was recorded) Session (Get) sessionId, ownerId, namespaceId, the summary text and the events, each with eventId, actorId, role, text, createdAt Session (Get Many) sessionId, ownerId, namespaceId, createdAt, updatedAt Namespace namespaceId, name, scope, state, parentId, ownerId Summary view viewId, name, visibility, groupBy, state, outputFormat, refreshMode, updatedAt Summary view result viewId, status, stale, the text or data, computedAt, sourceMemoryCount, summarizedMemoryCount, truncated and, when present, sourceMemoryIds and errorCode

Switch Simplify off for the API's object as it came. Delete operations return { deleted: true } with the ID that was deleted.

Resource locators. The Namespace field of Namespace → Get, Update, Delete and Long-Term Memory → Move offers the store's namespaces from a list, or takes an ID or expression; the View field of Summary View does the same for the store's views.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The node turns the API's Problem Details into n8n errors: the server's detail becomes the message and title (HTTP n) the description. A 404 with the resource-not-found type is the only "not found" the node recognises; a read-only API key answers 403. With Continue On Fail on, the error lands on the item and the workflow can branch on it.

docs.title: Chat Memory
docs.text:
Redis Agent Chat Memory connects to the Memory input of an AI Agent.

Loading history. The node returns the session's recent turns to the AI Agent. When enabled, they are preceded by the server-maintained summary of older turns, by a summary view's briefing on the user, and by long-term memories recalled for the current message. The Chat Trigger's Load Previous Session and n8n's Chat Memory Manager node get the turns only.

Saving history. The node appends each user and assistant message as a session event. Tool calls and tool results are not stored, so the most-voted n8n memory bug, the agent writing every tool output into memory, cannot happen here. Agent Memory then extracts long-term memories from the events asynchronously.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description Session ID Conversation identifier. Defaults to {{ $json.sessionId }} from the Chat Trigger. User ID The user the conversation belongs to. Extracted long-term memories are owned by this user. Recall Long-Term Memories Whether to search the user's long-term memories on every turn and give the results to the model (default off). The switch alone is enough: the query defaults to the current message. Recall Query Text to search with; shown when recall is on. Defaults to {{ $json.chatInput }}, the current message. Recall Limit Max memories to recall per turn (default 5); shown when recall is on. Options → Context Window Length How many past interactions are sent to the model (default 50, max 500). Keep it at least as high as the number of turns the server retains; see below. An expression must resolve to a whole number of 1 or more, or the run fails; an empty value means the default. Options → Include Summary Whether to prepend the summary of older turns (default on). Options → Namespace ID Binds the session to a namespace, so extracted memories land in it and recall searches only it. Options → Summary View ID ID of a summary view grouped by user. When set, the view's summary of the User ID is given to the model on every turn, before the session summary, once the server has computed it; until then, and if the view is gone, nothing is added. A result the server scopes to another user, or to no user, is ignored. Adds one request per turn. Empty by default. See Summary Views. Options → Verify Session Owner Whether to refuse a session that the server says belongs to another user (default off). See Sessions.

docs.title: What the model receives
docs.text:
In order, when each part is present:

  1. The summary view's briefing on the user (Summary View ID set and computed).
  2. The server's summary of the older turns of this session (Include Summary on).
  3. The long-term memories recalled for the current message (Recall Long-Term Memories on).
  4. The last Context Window Length turns the server has kept.

docs.title: Context window
docs.text:
The history is trimmed in up to three places:

  • The server keeps the recent turns of a session and folds older ones into the summary.
  • The node sends the model the last Context Window Length turns of what the server kept, preceded by the summary.
  • The AI Agent may trim once more, by tokens, if you set its Max Tokens From Memory.

The server is the main control: a turn it has retained but the summary does not cover yet is sent only if it falls inside the node's window. So keep Context Window Length at least as high as the number of turns your store retains before summarizing. The default of 50 is chosen for that; lower it only if your store retains fewer turns.

docs.title: Chat Memory Manager
docs.text:
n8n's own Chat Memory Manager node, which is not part of this package, works with this memory, with limits:

  • Get Many Messages and Insert Messages work.
  • Insert Messages with Override All Messages replaces the session: the summary is dropped and the new messages are extracted as new content.
  • Delete Messages with All Messages deletes the session.
  • Delete Messages with Last N is not supported: n8n implements it by deleting the session and re-inserting the kept turns through this node, which drops the summary and may extract the same facts again. The kept turns also get new event IDs, their actorId becomes the user of the deleting workflow, and that user becomes the session's owner.

To trim a session, use the action node's Session → Delete Event. To correct or remove what was learned, use Long-Term Memory → Search and Delete, or follow the Memory Sources guide.

docs.title: Users, Sessions and Namespaces
docs.text: Three identifiers decide who sees what. Get them right and the rest of the node is plumbing.

docs.title: User ID
docs.text:
Every long-term memory has an owner, and every search is scoped to one owner. The User ID parameter (ownerId in a workflow's JSON, on both nodes) is that owner.

  • On the chat memory node, the User ID is the user the conversation belongs to. Facts the server extracts from it are owned by this user.
  • On Search, only this user's memories are searched. On Create, the memory belongs to this user.
  • On tools, set it yourself from the workflow and never let the model fill it. A model-chosen User ID lets one user read another's memories.

Take the User ID from the authenticated trigger: a Telegram or Slack sender ID, a JWT claim on a Webhook, the n8n user on a Chat Trigger with authentication. Never from the request body.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session is one conversation: an ordered list of events (user, assistant and system messages) plus a server-maintained summary of the older ones. The chat memory node appends each user and assistant message as an event and reads the recent events back for the model. Tool calls and tool results are not stored.

Who may read a session. Anyone who sends a session ID can read and extend that session; the node cannot tell one client from another. Authentication belongs to the trigger, and the workflow should take the Session ID from the authenticated context or derive it from the user. The server records the first writer as the session's owner but accepts events from any user after that. Turn on Verify Session Owner on the chat memory node when every session belongs to exactly one user: the node then fails instead of mixing two users' turns. Leave it off for shared sessions, such as group chats.

Lifecycle. A session has no expiry of its own. Session → Delete removes it with its events and summary; Session → Delete Event removes one message and keeps the summary; Session → Get Many lists sessions, optionally by owner, with createdAt and updatedAt for idle clean-up. Deleting a session does not delete the long-term memories extracted from it; those are found with Long-Term Memory → Get Many and the Session ID filter. The session lifecycle example wires /reset, /forget me and a nightly clean-up.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
A namespace groups long-term memories. Without one, a user's memories are simply the user's. With one, several agents or channels can share the facts they learn about a customer while the User ID still keeps customers apart.

  • Namespace → Create takes a Name and a Scope: Shared (any user's memories may be placed there) or Personal (belongs to one user, set under Additional Fields). A Parent ID nests the namespace under another; the child inherits the parent's scope and user.
  • The chat memory node's Namespace ID option binds the session to a namespace: extracted memories land there, and recall searches only it.
  • Search, Get Many and Create take a Namespace ID option or field; Long-Term Memory → Move moves one memory to another namespace, chosen from the store's list.
  • Namespace → Update renames or archives; the API cannot make an archived namespace active again.

The shared memory example puts a sales agent and a support agent on one namespace.

docs.title: How they fit together
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U[User ID] -->|owns| M[Long-term memories]
    U -->|owns| S[Sessions]
    S -->|events are extracted into| M
    N[Namespace] -->|groups| M
    S -.->|bound to| N
    V[Summary view] -->|summarizes, grouped by user / session / namespace / type| M

A long-term memory records its ownerId, sessionId (when extracted from a session), namespaceId (when placed in one), memoryType, topics and createdAt, and carries its sources.

docs.title: Memory Sources
docs.text: Every long-term memory the server extracts can say where it came from: the session and the events, or the document revision, that produced it. This answers "why do you believe that?" for an agent and "which conversation produced this wrong fact?" for an operator, and it makes "forget everything from this thread" a two-step workflow. Corrections, audit and memory poisoning are rising concerns in the n8n community and in other memory vendors' issue trackers; no other n8n memory node exposes provenance.

docs.title: Include Sources
docs.text:
Search, Get and Get Many have an Include Sources switch (shown when Simplify is on). Each memory then carries sources, an array of:

Field Meaning sourceId ID of the source link. kind SESSION or DOCUMENT. sessionId For a session source, the session the memory was extracted from. documentId For a document source, the ingested document. eventIds For a session source, the events that produced the memory.

It costs no extra request: the data is already in the response. This is the cheapest way to let a tool-using agent cite where a memory came from: "you told the support bot this on 12 May".

docs.title: Get Sources
docs.text:
Long-Term Memory → Get Sources lists the sources of one Memory ID, one item per source, with more detail: revision for documents, eventIds across every evidence entry, evidenceCount (the number of evidence entries, not of events) and capturedAt (when the first evidence entry was recorded). With Simplify off, the raw link includes the evidence arrays and the producer that recorded them (iris-memory-extraction for the server's extractor).

A memory created directly with Create has no sources: nothing extracted it.

docs.title: From a source to the evidence
docs.text:
Combine three operations to show the exact messages behind a memory:

flowchart LR
    S[Search<br/>Include Sources] --> G[Get Sources]
    G --> F{kind = SESSION}
    F --> R[Session → Get<br/>Include Summarized Events]
    R --> E[Filter events<br/>by eventIds]

Session → Get with Include Summarized Events on returns every event, including the older ones the summary already covers, so the evidence is found even after the session was summarized. The trace example wraps this in a webhook.

docs.title: Correct a memory
docs.text: A wrong or outdated fact ("lives in Berlin" after a move to Madrid) is fixed with Long-Term Memory → Update and a new Text. The memory keeps its ID and sources. Deleting it instead and letting the next conversation re-extract is also fine; the choice depends on whether the old sources still matter for audit.

docs.title: Forget a thread
docs.text:
To remove a conversation and what was learned from it, for example one that came from an untrusted channel:

  1. Session → Delete the session.
  2. Long-Term Memory → Get Many with the Session ID and User ID filters, Return All.
  3. Long-Term Memory → Delete each result.

Deleting the session alone does not delete the memories extracted from it: they are the user's long-term facts and stay until deleted. The same three steps, with the User ID filter alone and Session → Get Many by owner, implement "forget me".

docs.title: Summary Views
docs.text:
A summary view is a standing summary the server keeps over long-term memories, one per group: per user, session, namespace or memory type. It gives a workflow a "standing briefing" in one call, where template authors otherwise chain dozens of nodes or have a human type the note: the hand-off packet at escalation, the weekly "what did the agent learn about each customer" digest, the state a scheduled agent reads at the start of each run, a tutor's per-student progress. No other n8n memory integration offers shared, grouped, on-demand summaries.

Note

Summary views must be enabled on the store.

docs.title: Define a view
docs.text:
Summary View → Create takes:

Field Meaning Name A name for the view, for example customer-briefing. Group By One summary per distinct value of these keys: User, Session, Namespace, Memory Type, or a combination. Get Result then selects a summary with the same keys. Output Format Text (prose) or Structured (an object that follows the Schema under Additional Fields, for example { "fields": [...] } with dietary, city, language). Instructions What the summary should focus on, in plain language. Refresh Mode Manual: a summary is computed only after Refresh. Continuous: recomputed whenever the memories change, at a model call per change; Debounce and Reconcile Interval under Additional Fields tune it. Additional Fields Filters (User ID, Namespace ID, Session ID, Memory Type, Topics, a Time Window in seconds), Max Partitions (how many groups the server keeps), Visibility (Private or Shared with the store's other API keys), Description.

Update changes any of these, plus State (Active or Disabled; a disabled view keeps its results) and the switches Clear Filter and Clear Time Window. Delete removes the view and its results.

docs.title: Read a group
docs.text:
Get Result reads one group's summary. Give the keys the view groups by under Group, for example the User ID for a view grouped by user. The result's status is:

Status Meaning COLD Never computed for this group. PENDING, REFRESHING Being computed. READY text (or data) holds the summary; computedAt says when. EMPTY Computed, but the group has no memories to summarize. FAILED The server could not compute it; errorCode says why.

stale is true when memories changed since computedAt. sourceMemoryCount and summarizedMemoryCount say how much went in; truncated warns that not everything fit. Include Source Memory IDs under Options adds the IDs the summary was computed from.

Wait For Result polls every two seconds until the status is READY, EMPTY or FAILED, and fails after Max Wait seconds (default 60). A FAILED result is returned as an item with its errorCode, not thrown.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text: Refresh asks the server to compute again. Target Partition recomputes one group, selected by the Group keys, and can Wait For Result like Get Result does, so "refresh this customer and give me the text" is one node. Full recomputes every group and returns { viewId, target, accepted } at once; read the groups afterwards with Get Result and Wait For Result.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
• Hand-off packet. At escalation, Refresh (Partition, Wait For Result) for the customer's User ID, then paste text into the ticket. The hand-off example does this from a webhook.
  • Weekly digest. Schedule → Refresh (Full) → one Get Result per known user → join the texts. Same example.
  • Standing briefing for an agent. Set the chat memory node's Summary View ID option to a view grouped by user: the model gets the user's briefing on every turn, before the session summary, once it is computed. Adds one request per turn.
  • "What do you know about me?" A Redis Agent Memory Tool set to Get Result with the view and the User ID group pinned answers in one call.
  • Structured profile fields. A Structured view with a schema fills CRM columns from conversations without a parsing step.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Every parameter of Redis Agent Chat Memory and Redis Agent Memory, by resource and operation. Redis Agent Memory Tool is the action node in the AI Agent's Tool picker and has the same parameters. Parameter names in code are the keys in a workflow's JSON, useful when you set them by expression or edit an exported workflow.

docs.title: Redis Agent Chat Memory
docs.text: Parameter Key Default Description Session ID sessionId {{ $json.sessionId }} Conversation identifier. User ID ownerId The user the conversation belongs to. Extracted long-term memories are owned by this user. Recall Long-Term Memories recallLongTermMemories off Search the user's long-term memories on every turn and give the results to the model. Recall Query recallQuery {{ $json.chatInput }} Text to search long-term memories with. Shown when recall is on. Recall Limit recallLimit 5 Max number of long-term memories to recall per turn. Options → Context Window Length options.windowSize 50 How many past interactions are sent to the model (1–500). Options → Include Summary options.includeSummary on Prepend the server's summary of older turns. Options → Namespace ID options.namespaceId Bind the session to a namespace. Options → Summary View ID options.summaryViewId Give the model this view's summary of the user on every turn. Options → Verify Session Owner options.verifyOwner off Refuse a session the server says belongs to another user.

docs.title: Redis Agent Memory
docs.text: Resource is resource, operation is operation. The resource values are longTermMemory, session, namespace and summaryView.

docs.title: Search (search)
docs.text:
Search a user's long-term memories by meaning.

Parameter Key Required Description Query query yes Text to search for. Memories are ranked by meaning, not by keyword. User ID ownerId yes Only memories owned by this user are searched. Limit limit Max number of results, 1–100 (default 50). Simplify simple Default on. Include Sources includeSources Keep where each memory came from, in short form. Shown when Simplify is on. Options → Memory Type options.memoryType Only memories of this type, built-in or custom. Options → Namespace ID options.namespaceId Only memories in this namespace. Options → Session ID options.sessionId Only memories extracted from this session. Options → Similarity Threshold options.similarityThreshold Minimum similarity, 0–1. 0 returns the closest matches regardless of score. Options → Topics options.topics Only memories tagged with any of these topics, comma-separated.

docs.title: Get Many (getAll)
docs.text:
List long-term memories that match the filters. At least one filter is required.

Parameter Key Description Return All returnAll Return every result instead of the first Limit. Limit limit Max number of results, 1–100 (default 50). Simplify simple Default on. Include Sources includeSources As on Search. Filters → Memory Type filters.memoryType Only memories of this type. Filters → Namespace ID filters.namespaceId Only memories in this namespace. Filters → Session ID filters.sessionId Only memories extracted from this session. Filters → Topics filters.topics Any of these topics, comma-separated. Filters → User ID filters.ownerId Only memories owned by this user.

docs.title: Create (create)
docs.text:
Store a fact as a long-term memory of a user. Creating the same Memory ID again replaces the memory with the fields given.

Parameter Key Required Description Text text yes The fact to remember, in plain language. User ID ownerId yes Owner of the memory. Simplify simple Default on. Additional Fields → Memory ID additionalFields.memoryId Letters, digits and dashes. Generated when empty. Additional Fields → Memory Type additionalFields.memoryType Built-in or a custom type registered on the store. Additional Fields → Namespace ID additionalFields.namespaceId Namespace to place the memory in. Additional Fields → Session ID additionalFields.sessionId Session the memory came from. Additional Fields → Topics additionalFields.topics Topic tags, comma-separated.

docs.title: Get (get)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Memory ID memoryId yes ID of the memory. Simplify simple Default on. Include Sources includeSources As on Search.

docs.title: Get Sources (getSources)
docs.text:
List the sessions or documents a memory was extracted from, with the evidence. One output item per source.

Parameter Key Required Description Memory ID memoryId yes ID of the memory. Return All returnAll Return every source. Limit limit Max number of sources, 1–100 (default 50). Simplify simple Default on.

docs.title: Update (update)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Memory ID memoryId yes ID of the memory. Simplify simple Default on. Update Fields → Memory Type updateFields.memoryType New type. Update Fields → Namespace ID updateFields.namespaceId New namespace. Update Fields → Session ID updateFields.sessionId New source session. Update Fields → Text updateFields.text New content. Update Fields → Topics updateFields.topics Replaces the existing topics. Update Fields → User ID updateFields.ownerId New owner.

docs.title: Delete (delete)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Memory ID memoryId yes ID of the memory. Returns { deleted: true, memoryId }.

docs.title: Move (move)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Memory ID memoryId yes ID of the memory. Namespace namespaceId yes Resource locator: from the store's list (mode: "list") or an ID or expression (mode: "id").

docs.title: Get (get)
docs.text:
Get the events and summary of a session.

Parameter Key Required Description Session ID sessionId yes ID of the session. Simplify simple Default on. Options → Include Summarized Events options.includeSummarisedEvents Also return the older events the summary already covers.

docs.title: Get Many (getAll)
docs.text:
List sessions. Without a filter, every session on the store. Each item has sessionId, ownerId, namespaceId, createdAt and updatedAt.

Parameter Key Description Return All returnAll Return every session. Limit limit Max number of sessions (default 50). Filters → User ID filters.ownerId Only sessions owned by this user.

docs.title: Delete (delete)
docs.text:
Delete a session with its events and summary. Long-term memories extracted from it stay.

Parameter Key Required Description Session ID sessionId yes Returns { deleted: true, sessionId }.

docs.title: Add Event (addEvent)
docs.text:
Append a message to a session. The session is created when it does not exist.

Parameter Key Required Description Session ID sessionId yes ID of the session. User ID ownerId yes User the message belongs to. Extracted memories are owned by this user. Role role USER (default), ASSISTANT or SYSTEM. Text text yes Content of the message. Additional Fields → Created At additionalFields.createdAt When the message was said. Defaults to now. Additional Fields → Namespace ID additionalFields.namespaceId Bind the session to a namespace.

docs.title: Delete Event (deleteEvent)
docs.text:
Delete one event, keeping the rest and the summary.

Parameter Key Required Description Session ID sessionId yes ID of the session. Event ID eventId yes ID of the event. Session → Get returns the IDs.

docs.title: Create (create)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Name name yes Name of the namespace. Scope scope SHARED (default) or PERSONAL. Ignored when Parent ID is set: a child inherits its parent's scope. Simplify simple Default on. Additional Fields → Parent ID additionalFields.parentId Nest under this namespace. Additional Fields → User ID additionalFields.ownerId Owner, for personal namespaces.

docs.title: Get (get), Update (update), Delete (delete)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Namespace namespaceId yes Resource locator: list, or ID or expression. Simplify simple Get and Update. Default on. Update Fields → Name updateFields.name New name. Update Fields → Archive updateFields.archive Archive the namespace. The API cannot make an archived namespace active again.

docs.title: Get Many (getAll)
docs.text: Parameter Key Description Return All returnAll Return every namespace. Limit limit Max number (default 50). Simplify simple Default on.

docs.title: Get Result (getResult)
docs.text:
Read the summary of one group.

Parameter Key Required Description View viewId yes Resource locator: list, or ID or expression. Group → User ID / Session ID / Namespace ID / Memory Type group.ownerId, group.sessionId, group.namespaceId, group.memoryType The keys the view groups by. Wait For Result waitForResult Poll every 2 seconds until READY, EMPTY or FAILED. Max Wait (Seconds) maxWaitSeconds Fail after this long (default 60). Shown when waiting. Options → Include Source Memory IDs options.includeSourceMemoryIds Return the IDs of the memories the summary was computed from. Simplify simple Default on.

docs.title: Refresh (refresh)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description View viewId yes Resource locator. Target target PARTITION (default): one group, selected by Group. FULL: every group. Group → … group.* For a Partition refresh, the group to recompute. Wait For Result, Max Wait waitForResult, maxWaitSeconds Partition only. Simplify simple Default on.

docs.title: Create (create)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description Name name yes Name of the view. Group By groupBy yes Array of ownerId, sessionId, namespaceId, memoryType (default ["ownerId"]). Output Format outputFormat TEXT (default) or STRUCTURED. Instructions instructions What the summary should focus on. Refresh Mode refreshMode MANUAL (default) or CONTINUOUS. Simplify simple Default on. Additional Fields additionalFields.* debounceSeconds, description, maxPartitions, memoryType, namespaceId, reconcileIntervalSeconds, schema (JSON, { "fields": [...] }), sessionId, timeWindowSeconds, topics, ownerId, visibility (PRIVATE default, or SHARED).

docs.title: Get (get), Delete (delete)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description View viewId yes Resource locator. Simplify simple Get only. Default on.

docs.title: Get Many (getAll)
docs.text: Parameter Key Description Return All returnAll Return every view. Limit limit Max number (default 50). Simplify simple Default on.

docs.title: Update (update)
docs.text: Parameter Key Required Description View viewId yes Resource locator. Simplify simple Default on. Update Fields updateFields.* Every Create field (name, groupBy, outputFormat, instructions, refreshMode and the Additional Fields) plus state (ACTIVE or DISABLED), clearFilter and clearTimeWindow.

docs.title: Credential
docs.text: Redis Agent Memory API (redisAgentMemoryApi): serverUrl (host only; the nodes add /iris/data/v1/agent-memory), storeId, apiKey. The credential test calls the store's health endpoint.
